opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of those questions that sounds like a small implementation detail but ends up mattering a lot in practice.

The way I think about it is in terms of what behavior you want from the student when it **doesn't have the capacity to fully represent the teacher**, which is basically always the case when there's a big size gap.

**Forward KL**, KL(teacher || student), which is what standard distillation does, is *mode-covering*. The student gets penalized heavily wherever the teacher puts mass and the student doesn't. So a small student tries to spread probability over everything the teacher considers plausible. If the student is too small to do that well, you get a kind of smeared-out distribution. It puts mass in regions the teacher would never actually generate, and at sampling time that shows up as incoherent or hallucinated continuations.

**Reverse KL**, KL(student || teacher), is *mode-seeking*. The student is penalized for putting mass where the teacher doesn't, but it's allowed to ignore some of the teacher's modes. So a capacity-limited student tends to commit to a few high-quality modes and do those well. For a lot of generation tasks, especially where you care about the quality of a single sample more than diversity, that's often the better trade-off.

There's no universal answer, though. It depends on the task and on how you're decoding. If you're sampling at higher temperature and want diversity, forward KL or something in between can be better. If you're doing greedy or low-temperature decoding on something like reasoning or summarization, mode-seeking objectives tend to shine. That's partly why it's useful to think of a family of divergences, like generalized Jensen-Shannon, where you interpolate between the two and treat the direction as a hyperparameter you actually tune rather than a fixed choice.

The thing I'd emphasize even more than the divergence direction, though, is **whose samples you compute the loss on**. Classic distillation trains on fixed data or teacher-generated sequences, so there's a train-inference mismatch. At test time the student conditions on its *own* prefixes, which can drift into states it never saw during training. If you instead sample from the student and have the teacher give token-level feedback on those student-generated sequences, which is on-policy distillation, you directly fix that exposure-bias problem. On-policy data and a mode-seeking divergence also fit together naturally, because reverse KL is literally an expectation under the student's distribution.

So my practical recipe would be: start on-policy if you can afford the student sampling, treat the divergence as something to tune, and expect mode-seeking variants to do well when the student is much smaller than the teacher and you care about sample quality.

r001.rationale: It says a capacity-limited student may spread probability broadly and put mass in regions the teacher would never generate.

r002.rationale: It explains that reverse KL can let the student ignore teacher modes and commit to a few high-quality modes.

r003.rationale: It identifies forward KL as mode-covering and says standard distillation uses it; it also describes classic distillation on fixed data or teacher-generated sequences.

r004.rationale: It says on-policy distillation and a mode-seeking divergence fit together naturally because reverse KL is an expectation under the student, but does not clearly identify on-policy distillation as optimizing mode-seeking KL.

r005.rationale: It frames the choice as a tradeoff between diversity and single-sample quality, recommending forward KL for diversity and mode-seeking objectives for quality-focused tasks.

r006.rationale: It recommends tuning the divergence and mentions interpolation, but does not recommend an approximately equal mixture as the default when the tradeoff is unclear.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I spent a lot of time on, and the short answer is: it depends on what you want the student to do, and whether the student actually has the capacity to match the teacher.

Let me back up. The standard way people do distillation, going back to Hinton, is you minimize the forward KL, KL of teacher from student. You take the teacher's distribution and you ask the student to cover it. The problem is that forward KL is mean-seeking. If the teacher puts mass on ten different modes and your student is too small to represent all ten, forward KL forces the student to spread its probability mass across all of them, and it ends up putting mass in the gaps between modes. At inference time, when you're sampling or decoding autoregressively, you're going to visit those gaps and generate stuff the teacher would never say. You get low-quality, sort of hedgy outputs.

Reverse KL flips that. It's mode-seeking. You're sampling from the student and asking, how surprised is the teacher by what I just produced? The student can concentrate on a subset of the teacher's modes and be penalized very little for ignoring the rest. For a capacity-limited student that's usually what you want. It's the same reason RLHF implicitly uses reverse KL as its regularizer: you want the policy to stay in high-probability regions of the reference, not to cover everything the reference might do.

The other thing that matters a lot, and this was really the core of the on-policy distillation work, is whose samples you train on. Classic distillation trains on a fixed dataset, often teacher-generated. But the student then sees its own outputs at inference, and those are different from the teacher's outputs. That's exposure bias, and it compounds over long sequences. If you instead sample from the student and have the teacher provide token-level feedback on those samples, you're training on the distribution the student will actually encounter. That's where reverse KL falls out naturally, because you're already drawing from the student.

Now, forward KL isn't wrong. If you have a student that's large enough to roughly match the teacher, or you care about diversity and calibration, forward KL is fine, and it's often more stable early in training because you're learning from clean teacher data. In practice I think of them as points on a spectrum. There are generalized divergences, Jensen-Shannon with an interpolation parameter, where you can tune how mode-seeking you are. Our experience was that for small students on tasks like summarization or translation, mode-seeking objectives on student-generated sequences won pretty consistently, both on metrics and on how the outputs actually read. For tasks where the answer space is small and you mostly want calibrated probabilities, the difference shrinks.

One more practical note: reverse KL on your own samples is noisier, because you're doing Monte Carlo over student outputs rather than averaging over a fixed dataset. So you often see people mix in some supervised data or anneal from forward to reverse. That's not a theoretical requirement, it's just variance management.

So the mental model: ask whether you want the student to be a faithful but blurry approximation of the teacher, or a sharp approximation of part of the teacher. The first is forward, the second is reverse. And for small models that get deployed and sampled from, I'd lean reverse, on-policy.

r001.rationale: It says forward KL can make a capacity-limited student spread probability across teacher modes and put mass in the gaps between them, where the teacher would not generate.

r002.rationale: It explains that reverse KL lets the student concentrate on a subset of the teacher’s modes while ignoring the rest.

r003.rationale: It identifies standard distillation as minimizing forward KL and explains that this asks the student to cover the teacher’s distribution.

r004.rationale: It says student-sampled, on-policy distillation naturally uses reverse KL.

r005.rationale: It contrasts forward KL’s diversity and calibration benefits with mode-seeking objectives’ stronger task metrics and output quality on small students.

r006.rationale: It mentions tuning generalized divergences and mixing supervised data, but does not recommend an approximately equal mixture of forward and reverse KL as a default.

astra-6.text:
I think about it in terms of what you want the student to do when it can’t represent everything the teacher knows. With forward KL—KL from the teacher to the student—you’re penalizing the student for assigning low probability to things the teacher considers plausible. That encourages coverage of the teacher’s distribution. The standard example is training the student on teacher-generated responses using maximum likelihood.

With reverse KL—from the student to the teacher—you’re sampling from the student and penalizing it for putting probability on things the teacher considers unlikely. That tends to be more mode-seeking: the student can concentrate on a subset of good responses rather than trying to cover every possibility. For a smaller model, that can be a useful tradeoff.

But I’d separate the direction of KL from the question of where your training trajectories come from. If the student only sees teacher trajectories during training, it may not learn what to do in the states it reaches through its own mistakes. Training on student-generated trajectories lets the teacher provide feedback exactly where the student needs it. You can use different divergence objectives on those trajectories, so it’s not simply that on-policy distillation means reverse KL.

So I wouldn’t say one direction is universally better. I’d look at student capacity, whether diversity or concentrating on high-quality answers matters more, and how closely the training distribution matches what the student encounters at inference.

r001.rationale: The response says forward KL encourages coverage of teacher-plausible outputs, but does not explain that a capacity-limited student may then assign substantial probability to regions the teacher considers unlikely.

r002.rationale: It says reverse KL can concentrate on a subset of good responses, but does not clearly state that the student can fit a single teacher mode while neglecting the others.

r003.rationale: It identifies forward KL as the teacher-to-student direction and gives maximum-likelihood training on teacher-generated responses as the standard example, communicating supervised distillation with mode-covering KL.

r004.rationale: The response explicitly says on-policy distillation does not necessarily mean reverse KL and that different divergence objectives can be used on student-generated trajectories.

r005.rationale: It frames the practical choice as coverage and diversity versus concentrating on high-quality responses, which communicates a tradeoff between output diversity and performance.

r006.rationale: It gives no recommendation to mix the two KL directions approximately equally as a default.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it in terms of which mistakes you want the student to avoid. If you minimize forward KL, KL from the teacher to the student, you’re penalizing the student for failing to put probability mass wherever the teacher does. That’s a mode-covering objective. Standard distillation on teacher-generated responses is essentially doing that: the student learns to imitate samples from the teacher.

With reverse KL, KL from the student to the teacher, you sample from the student and ask how much probability the teacher assigns to those outputs. That tends to be mode-seeking. The student can focus on a subset of responses it can model well, but it gets penalized for generating things the teacher considers unlikely.

For a smaller student, that distinction matters because it may not have the capacity to represent the teacher’s entire distribution. Covering everything can be a difficult objective. Reverse KL gives it more freedom to concentrate, but you can lose diversity, and exploration becomes an issue: you’re learning from what the student already generates.

So I wouldn’t say one direction is universally better. I’d look at the capacity gap, whether diversity matters for the application, and whether we can afford teacher feedback on student-generated trajectories. The direction of KL and the distribution you train on are both important parts of that choice.

r001.rationale: The response says forward KL penalizes missing teacher-supported mass and can be difficult for a limited-capacity student. It does not say this makes the student assign substantial probability to regions the teacher considers unlikely.

r002.rationale: It says reverse KL is mode-seeking and lets the student focus on a subset of responses it can model well, while penalizing outputs the teacher considers unlikely.

r003.rationale: It identifies standard distillation on teacher-generated responses as essentially minimizing forward KL by learning to imitate teacher samples.

r004.rationale: It describes reverse KL using student-generated samples, but does not identify on-policy distillation as optimizing that mode-seeking objective.

r005.rationale: It discusses diversity as a consideration, but does not describe a tradeoff between output diversity and task performance.

r006.rationale: It does not recommend mixing the two KL directions as a default.
